aspects: Vaccines expose the body to an antigen without causing the actual disease
Innate immune cells detect the antigen and activate T and B cells
B cells make antibodies while T cells coordinate and kill infected cells
Memory B and T cells form, enabling faster stronger response on later exposure
Different vaccine types (live, inactivated, subunit, mRNA) present antigens to trigger this response
Boosters are needed because antibodies and memory wane or pathogens mutate to evade immunity

evaluation_claims.text: The immune system is divided into two collaborating subsystems: innate immunity and adaptive immunity.
Innate immunity serves as the immediate first-line defense.
Innate immunity reacts non-specifically by identifying conserved molecular patterns shared across microorganisms using pattern recognition receptors.
Adaptive immunity is pathogen-specific.
Adaptive immunity involves B cells and T cells, which recognize unique subregions on antigens known as epitopes.
An antigen is a foreign substance that stimulates an immune response, and vaccines use antigens to safely build active immunization without causing active disease.

After vaccine administration, components of the innate immune system recognize vaccine antigens, bind to them, and aid their engulfment by antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages, monocytes, or dendritic cells.
Antigen-presenting cells process antigens and display them alongside major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins on their surface.
Antigen presentation, together with cytokines and co-stimulatory molecules produced by the innate system, triggers adaptive immune activation.
Adaptive activation stimulates clonal expansion, causing specific B cells and T cells to multiply.
B cells generate circulating antibodies that bind and neutralize the pathogen.
A population of pathogen-specific memory B and T cells is formed and retained in the body after vaccination.
Memory cells respond much faster than in an unexposed individual when the real pathogen enters the host later, helping prevent severe illness.
A booster is an additional vaccine dose administered sometime after primary immunization to boost the immune response.
Over time, circulating antibody levels can decrease and vaccine-induced immunity can wane.
When antibody quantities fall below protective levels, a person becomes more susceptible to breakthrough infection.
A booster shot activates memory B cells to rapidly rebuild the quantity and quality of antibodies within a few days.
For measles, a two-dose childhood series establishes lifelong immunity.
The tetanus vaccine requires a booster every ten years to maintain strong protection because antibody levels drop over time.
A Tdap booster is recommended during each pregnancy to help pass protection to newborns.
Additional boosters may be recommended in high-risk contexts such as healthcare work or travel to regions with low vaccination coverage.
When viruses mutate, original vaccine-induced protection can diminish.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, variants like Omicron evaded early vaccine-induced defenses, lowering initial protection against infection to around 35 percent.
A booster shot restored protection against Omicron infection to approximately 75 percent.
Public health authorities introduced updated, strain-matched booster shots formulated to target evolving variants.
Acquired immunity does not last equally long for all pathogens, and the reasons why some vaccines confer lifelong immunity while others fade are not completely understood.

Mathematical modeling shows that if booster doses are given too closely together before immunological memory is fully established, antibody gains are minimal compared to regimens with adequate time between shots.
Questions remain about the longevity and overall effectiveness of repeated boosters against rapidly mutating variants.

reference_verifications.rationale: Immune system divided into two main subsystems, innate and adaptive, which continually interact.
Innate provides a first line of defense.
Non-specific; recognizes conserved patterns via PRRs.
Adaptive actions are specific to the particular pathogenic agent.
B and T cells are part of adaptive immunity, but evidence does not mention epitopes or recognition of unique subregions on antigens.

Evidence says vaccines introduce a controlled antigen amount not strong enough to cause disease, and artificial active immunization doesn't produce active disease. The definition of antigen as a foreign substance stimulating an immune response is only loosely implied (c76f2fa4562b mentions foreign antigen).
Innate components opsonize/bind and aid engulfment by APCs such as macrophages or monocytes; dendritic cells are named as APCs in another source.
APCs process antigens and insert them with MHC protein onto the APC surface.
Co-stimulatory molecules and cytokines from innate cells affect adaptive T and B cells; APCs present antigens and provide co-stimulatory signals to initiate adaptive activation.
Antigen-specific B cells proliferate on antigen stimulation, and adaptive response involves clonal expansion of specific immune cells; T cells are mentioned as clonally expanding (CTL cells).

Evidence says B cells mature into plasma cells that produce antibodies, and IgG is a good neutralizing antibody; antibodies recognize antigen. The claim of circulating antibodies that bind and neutralize the pathogen is only partly and indirectly supported.
Vaccination builds memory B and T cells that remain in place; memory B cells are built after vaccination and remain for years.
Memory cells rapidly activate the response compared with the naive host, with mild or no symptoms; memory cells reduce severity of illness.
Evidence explicitly defines a booster dose as boosting the immune response sometime after primary immunization.
Evidence states antibody levels can naturally decrease and immunity from some vaccines can fade.
As antibody levels drop, the virus may infect the person; breakthrough cases occur as immunity wanes.
Boosters rebuild antibodies quickly, within a few days, because memory B cells respond quickly; quantity and quality increase.
A two-dose childhood vaccine achieves lifelong immunity from measles.
Tetanus boosters are recommended every ten years because the antigen response needs strengthening; antibody levels decrease over time.
Tdap booster recommended during each pregnancy to help protect newborns from pertussis.
UCLA says high-risk scenarios like health care work or travel to low-vaccination countries may require additional boosters.

Evidence says mutation rate may affect need for boosters and that original-strain vaccines have limited protection against Omicron, but no explicit statement that mutation diminishes protection generally.
Omicron evading vaccinated immune systems leaving people only 35% protected against infection over time.
With a Pfizer or Moderna booster, protection jumps to 75%.
Public health authorities introduced updated COVID-19 vaccines formulated to target circulating variants.
Evidence states experts don't completely understand why immunity lasts longer for some vaccines than others; measles lifelong vs Tdap booster.

Simulation: with 2-month separation memory not fully formed and GMTs didn't increase significantly; with 8 months, highest GMTs. Modeling is of inactivated COVID vaccine, but the claim is generally consistent.
States booster longevity, effectiveness, and potential to thwart the new variant are unknown. 'Repeated' boosters and 'rapidly mutating' are slight extrapolations.

citation_entailment_verifications.rationale: Evidence states the immune system can be divided into two main subsystems, innate and adaptive, which continually interact.
Innate immunity is continually functioning and provides a first-line of defense.
E-2dd69c444188 says responses are not specific and innate cells recognize conserved molecular patterns; E-aa55e04ec5b0 mentions pattern recognition receptors.
Evidence refers to the adaptive (pathogen-specific) immune response.

Evidence supports that epitopes are small subregions on antigens recognized by the immune system, and that T and B cells are adaptive. However, it does not explicitly state that B and T cells recognize epitopes (the epitope recognition is attributed to the innate system/B cells in detection).

Evidence says immunizations mimic stimulation without active disease and that active immunization can be achieved by vaccines, and mentions antigens/epitopes. But it never defines an antigen as a foreign substance stimulating an immune response, nor explicitly says vaccines use antigens.

E-68d2c1999171 supports innate components opsonizing/binding and aiding engulfment by APCs such as macrophages or monocytes. It does not mention dendritic cells in this role, and it does not say vaccine antigens specifically. E-d14496f6da86 mentions DCs only as being activated.
Evidence states APCs process antigens and insert the processed antigen with MHC protein onto the APC surface.

Evidence says co-stimulatory molecules and cytokines from innate cells affect T and B cells, and that APCs initiate adaptive activation. It does not explicitly say that antigen presentation together with these factors triggers adaptive activation.

Evidence says adaptive immune response activation is followed by clonal expansion of specific immune cells (mostly antibodies or CTL cells). It does not say B and T cells multiply, and it does not say activation stimulates the expansion.
Evidence says vaccines build antibodies and that sufficient antibodies fend off the virus, but does not say B cells generate circulating antibodies that bind and neutralize the pathogen.
Vaccination builds memory B and T cells that remain in place; pathogen-specific memory cells are maintained long-term.
Memory cells rapidly activate the response upon secondary infection with mild or no symptoms, and memory cells help prevent severe infection.
Evidence defines a booster dose as given sometime after primary immunization to boost the immune response.
States that over time antibody levels can decrease and immunity from some vaccines can fade.
Evidence says as antibody levels drop, the virus may infect the person, explaining breakthrough cases.
Boosters rebuild antibodies quickly within days because memory B cells respond quickly; quantity and quality increase.
Evidence states a two-dose childhood vaccine achieves lifelong measles immunity.
Tetanus boosters every ten years; antibody response needs strengthening and antibody levels decline over time per the sources.
Evidence states Tdap booster is recommended during each pregnancy to help protect newborns.
States high-risk scenarios like health care work or travel to low-vaccination countries may require additional boosters.
Evidence says vaccines against original strain have limited protection to Omicron and mutation may affect immunity duration, but not directly that mutation diminishes protection in general.
Omicron evades vaccinated immune systems leaving ~35% protection against infection over time; 'early' and 'initial' framing is slightly different (over time).
Booster of Pfizer or Moderna raises protection to 75%.
Public health authorities introduced updated COVID-19 vaccines formulated to target circulating variants.
Evidence says experts don't completely understand why acquired immunity lasts longer for some vaccines than others, with measles lifelong vs Tdap needing boosters.
Simulation: with 2-month separation, memory not fully formed and GMTs did not increase significantly; with 8 months, highest GMTs.
Evidence states booster longevity, effectiveness, and potential to thwart the new variant are unknown.

additional_metric_details.notes: All scores are Claude judgments, not verified ground truth. Repair effectiveness compares coverage/narration, not factual truth. No revision or no retrieval is N/A rather than zero.

metric_semantics.reference_evidence_support_percent: Evidence entailment within the frozen reference corpus; not factual accuracy.
metric_semantics.query_coverage_percent: Coverage of a fixed six-aspect checklist derived once per question from the question text and shared by all systems; missing/duplicate judge outputs are normalized against that fixed denominator.
metric_semantics.narration_input: Coverage, relevance, narration and grounded-requirement judgements use the complete script with [E-...] evidence markers removed; claim extraction and citation metrics use the marked script. Aspect scores are continuous in [0, 1].
metric_semantics.narration_quality_percent: Ten-dimension spoken educational narration score; excludes factual truth.
metric_semantics.citation_precision: Share of emitted citation IDs that are identified as supporting the claim when verification is restricted to cited passages.
metric_semantics.citation_recall: Share of all citation-required extracted factual claims that have at least one cited passage judged to support the claim.
metric_semantics.evaluation_estimated_llm_cost_usd: Evaluator telemetry. CLI mode uses Claude Code's reported list-price equivalent; API mode uses the configured Anthropic per-token rates.
